citations.quote: Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

derivations.claim: Suppose there is a bad disk. Put its boundary transverse to $\partial\Delta$, avoiding the finite set $s\cap\partial\Delta$, and its interior transverse to $\Delta$. All these intersections can be made finite: use finite coordinate patches on the compact disks and their boundaries, perturb their vertices in a sufficiently fine polygonal approximation, then smooth in smaller patches. These perturbations preserve embedding and the number of intersections with $s$. Among bad disks in this position choose $X$ minimizing $m=|\partial X\cap\partial\Delta|$, using [F1].

Remove all circle components of $X\cap\Delta$ without changing $\partial X$. For a circle innermost on one of the cut disks, its enclosed disk $Q$ has interior disjoint from $X$: an intersection arc cannot enter its interior without crossing the circle, since the arc endpoints lie on the boundary of that cut disk. Surger $X$ along two nearby copies of $Q$, retain the disk with the original boundary and discard the sphere. This produces an embedded disk after rounding, and reduces the number of intersection circles. The cut disks are mutually disjoint, so the surgery introduces no intersections with another member of $\Delta$. Finitely many repetitions leave only arcs. The boundary remains bad and its count $m$ unchanged.

Suppose these arcs are nonempty. Disjoint arcs cut a disk into subdisks with a tree as dual graph: adding one arc splits one component, so adds one vertex and one edge without creating a cycle. A finite tree with an edge has at least two leaves, as follows by taking the two ends of a longest simple edge path. Thus there are at least two outermost subdisks of $X\setminus\Delta$. Their boundary portions on $\partial X$ have disjoint interiors. At most one contains the possible single point of $\partial X\cap s$, so choose an outermost subdisk whose boundary portion $\alpha\subset\partial N$ misses $s$. It lies in the punctured boundary sphere of one cut ball, and its two endpoints lie on the boundary of one spot $v$.

Join the two endpoints by a simple arc inside $v$. Together with $\alpha$ this gives a simple closed curve on the ball's boundary sphere. If other spots occur on both sides, the graph obtained by deleting $v$ is disconnected: a path from a vertex on one side to one on the other must cross $\alpha$, because the joining arc is inside the deleted spot, yet the edges miss $\alpha$. This contradicts the no-cut-vertex hypothesis. Therefore one complementary disk has no other spot; removing its part in $v$ gives a disk $R$ in the punctured sphere, with boundary $\alpha$ and a subarc of $\partial v$. The interior of $R$ contains no suture arc. Such an arc could not cross $\alpha$, and, with no other spot available, both its ends would be on $v$, producing a loop at $v$. The loop-free hypothesis excludes this. Consequently $R$ is disjoint from $s$, including its spot-boundary interval, since the endpoints of $\alpha$ avoid $s$.

There is a boundary bigon disjoint from $s$ and with interior disjoint from $\partial X$, contained in $R$. If $\operatorname{int}R$ misses $\partial X$, take $R$ itself. Otherwise the portions of $\partial X$ in $R$ are disjoint proper arcs with both endpoints on its spot-boundary interval: none can cross $\alpha$, and the single closed curve $\partial X$ already contains $\alpha$, so there is no additional closed component inside $R$. Choose an arc cutting off a disk adjacent to that interval with no further such arcs inside. This smaller disk is the required bigon. Isotoping $\partial X$ across it removes two intersections with $\partial v$, and introduces none with any other spot boundary. The isotopy is supported away from $s$ and extends to a collar of $\partial N$, carrying the entire embedded disk $X$ with it. Hence it preserves badness, while decreasing $m$ by two, contrary to step 1.1. It follows that $X\cap\Delta$ has no arcs.

Now $X$ lies in one cut ball, and $\partial X$ is a circle in its boundary sphere avoiding all spots. If it meets $s$ once, exactly one edge of $G$ crosses this circle, exactly once. If there are spots on both sides, deleting that edge separates the graph into two nonempty vertex sets, making it a bridge. If all spots are on one side, every graph edge has both endpoints on that side and must cross the circle an even number of times, by entry and exit. Both possibilities contradict a single intersection. Thus $\partial X$ misses $s$. Connectedness of $G$ then forces all spots onto the same side of $\partial X$; otherwise an edge path between spots on opposite sides would meet the circle. The other complementary disk has no spots and no suture arcs: each such arc has its endpoints on spots and could not enter this disk without crossing $\partial X$. This is a disk in the original $\partial N\setminus s$ bounded by $\partial X$, contradicting badness.
Every possible bad disk has been excluded. Therefore every disk with at most one suture intersection has no such intersection and has boundary bounding a disk in $\partial N\setminus s$, as asserted.

citations.quote: A regular link diagram is **connected** when its underlying projection graph is connected. It is **alternating** when successive crossing visits along each component switch between overpasses and underpasses. It is **reduced** when no complementary region of the projection sphere has a crossing more than once on its boundary. A connected alternating diagram that is reduced is a **reduced alternating link diagram**.

For a link projection on $S^2$, a **checkerboard coloring** assigns one of two colors to each complementary region so that regions sharing an edge have different colors. Given such a coloring, the **black Tait graph** has one vertex for each black region and one edge for each crossing joining the two opposite black sectors at that crossing. The **white Tait graph** is defined by interchanging black and white. Loops and parallel edges are allowed.
For a connected regular link projection on $S^2$ with at least one crossing and either checkerboard coloring, both Tait graphs are connected.

Let $D$ be a connected alternating regular link diagram on an oriented projection sphere. Choose either checkerboard color. Put a disk in each region of that color and join the opposite colored sectors at every crossing by a half-twisted band, with the twist chosen so that the boundary follows the over-under diagram. After rounding corners these disks and bands form a compact connected embedded spanning surface $F$ for the represented link. If $D$ has crossings, let $G$ be the corresponding Tait graph and orient its edges arbitrarily. Under the retraction of $F$ onto $G$, write a rational homology class as the unique graph cycle $a=\sum_{e\in E(G)}a_e e$. There is a single sign $\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ such that
$$q(a)=\epsilon\sum_{e\in E(G)}a_e^2=\operatorname{lk}(c,\tau c)$$
for every oriented rational multicurve $c$ representing $a$, where $\tau c$ is its normal transfer. Thus $q$ is positive definite or negative definite on $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$. For a crossingless connected diagram, use either spanning disk and the zero-dimensional definite form.

Let $D$ be a connected reduced alternating diagram on a projection sphere, with $n>0$ crossings. Call such a diagram **diagrammatically prime** if every simple closed curve transverse to it in exactly two noncrossing points has a complementary disk containing no crossings. Then $D$ has a finite binary splitting tree whose leaves are connected reduced alternating diagrammatically prime diagrams with positive crossing counts. Each split cuts along a two-point curve having crossings on both sides and caps the two resulting diagram arcs by crossingless arcs in disks. The leaf crossing counts sum to $n$, so there are at most $n$ leaves. For either checkerboard color, the checkerboard surface of each parent is a geometric boundary connected sum of its two children's checkerboard surfaces: an explicitly constructed sphere meets the link twice and the surface in one arc, and closing the pieces by a standard disk in either capping ball gives the two child surfaces. A crossingless connected diagram instead has its single spanning disk and needs no splitting.

Let $N$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold with boundary, and let $s\subset\partial N$ be a finite disjoint union of smooth simple closed curves. Supply a finite family $\Delta$ of disjoint properly embedded disks such that cutting $N$ along $\Delta$ gives finitely many balls. Each cut ball has **spots**, the disk copies created by the cuts. Suppose $s$ is transverse to $\partial\Delta$ and each component of its cut image in a ball is an arc with both endpoints on spot boundaries. Collapse each spot to a vertex and regard these arcs as edges of a finite graph $G$ on the boundary sphere. Assume, for every cut ball, that $G$ has at least two vertices, is connected and has no loops, no bridges and no cut vertex; here the last condition means that deleting any vertex leaves a connected graph.

Then any properly embedded disk $X\subset N$ with $\partial X$ transverse to $s$ and $|\partial X\cap s|\le1$ satisfies $\partial X\cap s=\varnothing$, and its boundary bounds a disk in $\partial N\setminus s$. In particular there is no properly embedded disk whose boundary meets $s$ exactly once.

Let $F$ be a compact smoothly embedded spanning surface for a link $L\subset S^3$, supplied with a finite disk-and-band presentation. Let $E=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu L$, and regard $F_E=F\cap E$ as a properly embedded surface, with one boundary curve on each boundary torus of $E$. Suppose $F_E$ is geometrically incompressible: every embedded disk in $E$ whose interior misses $F_E$ and whose boundary lies in $F_E$ has boundary bounding a disk in $F_E$.

Cut $E$ along $F_E$ to obtain $N$. Its boundary contains the normal double cover $P$ of $F_E$ and, for each component of $L$, an annulus $A_i$ obtained by cutting its boundary torus along the boundary curve of $F_E$. Choose a core $s_i$ of each $A_i$, and put $s=\bigcup_i s_i$. If $F_E$ has an exterior boundary-compressing disk, meaning an embedded disk $X\subset E$ with boundary the union of an arc $\beta\subset F_E$ and an arc $\alpha\subset\partial E$, interior disjoint from $F_E\cup\partial E$, and with $\beta$ not boundary-parallel in $F_E$, then there is a properly embedded disk $\widetilde X\subset N$ whose boundary meets $s$ transversely in exactly one point. In particular, the absence of such one-suture disks, together with geometric incompressibility, implies geometric incompressibility and boundary-incompressibility in the link exterior.

derivations.claim: Fix one checkerboard, say black, and write $G_B,G_W$ for the embedded Tait graphs. Their usual spherical embeddings can be constructed inside the regions, joining opposite sectors through each crossing. Recover the projection from $G_W$ by putting a crossing in each edge and joining the neighboring edge ends around each vertex disk in cyclic order; these are exactly the original region sectors and diagram edges. This is its medial description, which does not use alternation. By [F1] both graphs are connected, and neither has a loop, since the opposite sectors at a crossing are distinct regions. Each graph has at least two vertices, because it has an edge and no loop.

Neither graph has a bridge. For example let $e$ be a white Tait edge at a crossing $c$, with endpoints the two white regions there. Choose one adjacent black region and follow the rest of its boundary from one side of $c$ back to the other. At each intervening crossing its two adjacent diagram edges abut the two opposite white sectors, so the successive white regions give a walk in $G_W$ between the endpoints of $e$. This walk avoids $e$, because reducedness prevents that black region from encountering $c$ again. Thus the endpoints remain connected after deleting $e$. Interchanging the colors proves the other case.

The graph $G_W$ has no cut vertex. Suppose $v$ were one. Each component of $G_W-v$ has a nonempty set of attaching edge ends on the boundary of a small vertex disk at $v$. The attachment sets of two distinct components cannot interlace cyclically: paths in those components joining the corresponding attachments, closed by their short attachment strips, would give disjoint crosscuts of the complementary disk with alternating endpoints, which is impossible by the entry-and-exit separation of a simple planar arc. Some component therefore occupies one consecutive interval of attaching edge ends. Here is a finite way to choose it: cut the cyclic order at any gap and choose a component whose first-to-last attachment interval has the fewest positions. If another component had an attachment strictly inside this interval, noninterlacing would force all its attachments inside, giving a shorter interval; a one-attachment component already supplies a consecutive interval. Hence the chosen interval contains only its own component's ends.

We construct a ball cut system for the checkerboard exterior. Thicken the planar black Tait spine into vertex balls and round edge tubes, and place each surface disk as a middle disk of its vertex ball and each half-twisted band inside its tube. Denote this thickening by $H$. It is the interval thickening of $F$, with $L$ on its vertical boundary. The complement of its interior is homeomorphic to the link exterior cut along $F$: shrink the normal intervals and round the boundary corners, with the annular cores corresponding to $L$ on $\partial H$. This gives the required sutured identification with $N$. The graph spine lies on the projection sphere. Each of its complementary faces contains one white region; a truncated face disk in the complement of the vertex balls and tubes is a proper disk of $N$. These disks are mutually disjoint. Cutting through all these face disks disconnects the complementary handlebody into its upper and lower balls: the two complementary hemispherical balls were connected only through the face-disk product collars, and cutting those collars at their middle disks removes precisely these connections. Thus the spot vertices of each ball are indexed by the white regions.

Take a thin planar neighborhood of this component and its attachment strips, meeting the vertex disk just along that interval, and fill its holes. No other component is trapped in a filled hole: it would need an attachment path to $v$ crossing the chosen component or its strips. Its frontier separates the selected component and its incident edges from all other components. In the medial description in step 1.1 this produces a two-point diagram curve: pass once across the two medial strands at the ends of the attaching interval, use an arc in the region of $v$ between them, and run the rest of the curve outside the selected neighborhood. The neighborhood can be chosen to contain all medial strands and crossings of its edges, so the rest of the curve misses the diagram. Both sides contain a crossing, since the chosen component and some other component each have an attaching edge. This contradicts [F3]. Thus $G_W-v$ is connected for every $v$. The same construction applies with black and white exchanged.

The suture graphs of these two balls are both $G_W$. We verify the tracing. In a crossing chart the chosen overpass lies above the sphere and the underpass below it. The corresponding band is a half-twisted strip; for one incidence sign a parametrization is $(u,v)\mapsto(u,v\cos(\pi u),v\sin(\pi u))$, $0\le u\le1$, with boundary strands $v=\pm1$. For the opposite sign reverse the height coordinate. Its two boundary strands run on opposite sides of the projection sphere. Along a projection edge joining crossing neighborhoods, alternation makes one end an overpass end and the other an underpass end. After a small isotopy in its own disjoint edge collar, the suture there changes height monotonically from positive to negative or conversely, crossing the boundary of the appropriate white face disk exactly once. This isotopy can be made on the boundary of $H$: the middle surface disk's boundary arc is moved slightly to either normal side in the vertex ball's boundary collar. The common incidence sign in [F2] ensures these choices agree with the two adjoining band charts. There are no other suture intersections with the face disks. In the upper ball each remaining suture arc is the overpass at one crossing with its two adjacent half-edge collars; its endpoints belong to the two opposite white sectors. In the lower ball the underpass connects the same opposite white sectors. Hence each crossing contributes exactly its edge of $G_W$ to each ball, and every suture segment has been included.

By steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 the graph $G_W$ has at least two vertices and is connected, loop-free, bridge-free and has no cut vertex. Steps 2.3 and 3.2 realize precisely these graphs in the two balls of a finite cut system. Apply [F4]. It proves the asserted zero- and one-suture disk property for the black checkerboard. The construction with the colors interchanged proves the same property for the white checkerboard. Any two choices of annular cores are isotopic within their annuli; extending these isotopies over a boundary collar of $N$ transports disks and their boundary disks. The asserted property therefore holds for every choice of the cores.

This implies geometric incompressibility of $F$. A geometric compressing disk in the link exterior lifts to a proper disk in $N$ whose boundary $\widetilde\gamma$ lies on the normal frontier and misses $s$. By step 4.1 it bounds a disk $Y$ in $\partial N\setminus s$. Each component of the latter surface is the normal double cover of $F$ with half-annular boundary collars attached. Since $Y$ is compact and its boundary lies on the frontier, push its portions in these collars back to obtain a disk on the normal double cover itself. Projection takes $\widetilde\gamma$ homeomorphically onto its simple closed original curve $\gamma$. This disk also projects injectively: its boundary is disjoint from its image under the deck involution; two disks with disjoint boundaries are either disjoint or nested, unless their union is a sphere component, as follows by separating along either boundary circle. Every component of this normal double cover has nonempty boundary, so the sphere alternative is excluded. Strict nesting of the disk and its deck translate is impossible, since applying the involution reverses the asserted strict inclusion. They are therefore disjoint. The projected disk in $F$ bounds $\gamma$, excluding a geometric compression.

Finally, if there were a geometric exterior boundary compression, the incompressibility in step 5.1 and [F5] would produce a one-suture disk in $N$, contrary to step 4.1. Hence both checkerboards are geometrically incompressible and boundary-incompressible.

derivations.claim: Suppose a bad disk exists. Put its boundary transverse to $\partial D$, avoiding the two points $s\cap\partial D$, and its interior transverse to $D$, with finite intersections. This can be done by a sufficiently small polygonal perturbation in finitely many coordinate patches, followed by smoothing, preserving the suture intersection count. Use [F1] to choose a bad disk $X$ minimizing $m=|\partial X\cap\partial D|$.

Remove intersection circles in $X\cap D$ by surgery on a disk innermost in $D$, retaining the disk with the original boundary and discarding the sphere. The innermost disk's interior misses $X$, since an intersection arc with endpoints on $\partial D$ could not enter it without crossing its boundary circle. Thus the replacement is embedded after rounding. It removes circles without changing $\partial X$ or $m$. After finitely many such replacements, $X\cap D$ consists of arcs.

If these arcs are nonempty, choose an outermost subdisk $X_0$ whose boundary portion $\alpha$ on $\partial X$ misses $s$. Such a choice exists because disjoint arcs in a disk have at least two outermost complementary disks, whereas $\partial X$ meets $s$ at most once. The remaining boundary portion is a proper arc $\beta$ in a copy $D_i$ of the gluing disk, and $X_0$ lies in $N_i$. Thus $\partial X_0=\alpha\cup\beta$, with the interior of $\alpha$ disjoint from $D_i$.

Holding the endpoints fixed, isotope $\beta$ in $D_i$ to an arc $\beta'$ meeting $\lambda_i$ at most once. Indeed, $\lambda_i$ divides $D_i$ into two disks. If the endpoints are on the same boundary interval, choose $\beta'$ in that disk; otherwise choose an arc crossing $\lambda_i$ once. Any two proper arcs in a disk with the same endpoints are isotopic relative to its boundary, by cutting off their successive innermost bigons. Extend this boundary isotopy to a collar in $N_i$, carrying $X_0$ to a proper disk $X_i$ with boundary $\alpha\cup\beta'$. We do not require the isotopy to avoid $s_i$; its final boundary has at most one suture intersection, because $\alpha$ misses $s_i$ and all intersections lie on $\beta'\cap\lambda_i$. The summand hypothesis therefore rules out the one-intersection case. In the zero-intersection case it supplies a disk $Y_i\subset\partial N_i\setminus s_i$ with boundary $\alpha\cup\beta'$.

The arc $\beta'$ divides $D_i$ into two disks, exactly one of which lies in $Y_i$. This follows by separating along $\partial Y_i$: it meets the interior of $D_i$ only along $\beta'$, with its two endpoints on $\partial D_i$, so one side of that arc lies inside $Y_i$ and the other outside. The side inside $Y_i$ misses $\lambda_i$, since $Y_i$ misses $s_i$. Remove this disk from $Y_i$. What remains is a disk $R$ in $\partial N_i\setminus\operatorname{int}D_i$, with boundary $\alpha$ and an interval of $\partial D_i$, and disjoint from $s_i$. It is therefore a boundary bigon in the original $\partial N$, disjoint from $s$.

If other portions of $\partial X$ enter $R$, they are disjoint arcs with both ends on its interval of $\partial D$: they cannot cross $\alpha$, and the single boundary circle $\partial X$ already contains $\alpha$, so there is no separate circle inside $R$. Take an innermost such arc and the disk it cuts off adjacent to that interval, or use $R$ if its interior already misses $\partial X$. Isotoping across this smaller bigon removes two intersections of $\partial X$ with $\partial D$, without changing its intersection with $s$. This boundary isotopy extends over a collar to the whole disk $X$, preserves badness and decreases $m$, a contradiction. Hence $X\cap D$ has no arcs.

Thus $X$ lies in one summand, and its boundary is disjoint from $D_i$. It meets $s_i$ in the same at-most-one points as it meets $s$. The summand hypothesis gives zero intersections and a disk $Y_i\subset\partial N_i\setminus s_i$ bounded by $\partial X$. This disk misses $D_i$: its boundary misses the connected disk $D_i$, so either the interior of $D_i$ lies in $Y_i$ or it is disjoint from $Y_i$; the first possibility would put $\lambda_i\subset s_i$ inside $Y_i$. Therefore $Y_i$ is also a disk in $\partial N\setminus s$, contradicting badness.
No bad disk exists. This is exactly the required preservation of the zero- and one-suture disk property under the specified boundary sum.

Let $D$ be a connected reduced alternating spherical diagram with at least one crossing. Assume it is diagrammatically prime: every simple closed curve transverse to $D$ in exactly two noncrossing points has a complementary disk containing no crossings. For either checkerboard surface $F$ spanning the represented link $L$, let $N$ be the link exterior cut along $F$, and let $s$ be the union of the core curves of its boundary annuli coming from the boundary tori. Every properly embedded disk $X\subset N$ with $|\partial X\cap s|\le1$ has $\partial X\cap s=\varnothing$ and bounds a disk along its boundary in $\partial N\setminus s$. Consequently $F$ is geometrically incompressible and boundary-incompressible as a properly embedded surface in the link exterior. These assertions apply to both checkerboard colors.

For $i=1,2$, let $N_i$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold with boundary, with a finite union $s_i$ of disjoint simple closed curves in its boundary and a marked boundary disk $D_i$. Suppose $s_i\cap D_i$ is exactly one properly embedded arc $\lambda_i$. Glue the disks by a diffeomorphism carrying $\lambda_1$ to $\lambda_2$, and round corners to obtain $N=N_1\cup_D N_2$. Let $s\subset\partial N$ be the union of the unglued portions of the $s_i$, joined at the two matched endpoints; thus the interior arcs $\lambda_i$ are removed.

Assume that in each summand every properly embedded disk $Y$ with $|\partial Y\cap s_i|\le1$ has no such intersection and has boundary bounding a disk in $\partial N_i\setminus s_i$. Then every properly embedded disk $X\subset N$ with $|\partial X\cap s|\le1$ likewise has no such intersection and has boundary bounding a disk in $\partial N\setminus s$.

Let $F$ be a compact smoothly embedded spanning surface for a link $L\subset S^3$, supplied with a finite disk-and-band presentation. Let $E=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu L$, and regard $F_E=F\cap E$ as a properly embedded surface, with one boundary curve on each boundary torus of $E$. Suppose $F_E$ is geometrically incompressible: every embedded disk in $E$ whose interior misses $F_E$ and whose boundary lies in $F_E$ has boundary bounding a disk in $F_E$.

Cut $E$ along $F_E$ to obtain $N$. Its boundary contains the normal double cover $P$ of $F_E$ and, for each component of $L$, an annulus $A_i$ obtained by cutting its boundary torus along the boundary curve of $F_E$. Choose a core $s_i$ of each $A_i$, and put $s=\bigcup_i s_i$. If $F_E$ has an exterior boundary-compressing disk, meaning an embedded disk $X\subset E$ with boundary the union of an arc $\beta\subset F_E$ and an arc $\alpha\subset\partial E$, interior disjoint from $F_E\cup\partial E$, and with $\beta$ not boundary-parallel in $F_E$, then there is a properly embedded disk $\widetilde X\subset N$ whose boundary meets $s$ transversely in exactly one point. derivations.claim: For a crossingless connected diagram, $F$ is a disk, and the cut-open exterior is a ball whose suture is one circle dividing its boundary into two disks. A circle bounding a proper disk in this ball cannot meet that suture exactly once, because a closed curve crosses a separating circle an even number of times. If it misses the suture, it lies in one of the two complementary disks and bounds a disk there. This is the same stronger disk property.

Suppose first that the diagram has crossings. Use [F2] to obtain its finite splitting tree, retaining the specified color at every node. Each node surface comes with the standard capping disks and link arcs in the product balls used in its split, so no comparison of abstract prime decompositions is needed.

For each such surface boundary sum, its complementary sutured manifold is the boundary sum in [F4]. This can be checked in a boundary-arc chart: take the surface locally as $\{z=0,y\ge0\}$, with boundary on the $x$-axis, and its interval thickening locally as $\{y\ge0,|z|\le\varepsilon\}$. Its vertical boundary is $y=0$, and the link is the arc $z=0$ in that boundary. Choose a small disk there bisected by this arc. Gluing the two complementary manifolds along these disks removes the two marked link arcs and joins their exterior portions at the endpoints, while the two middle surfaces are joined by the boundary-sum strip. The coordinates round to smooth collars; away from them nothing changes. In the projection-product construction in [F2] the marked disks are precisely the complementary disks of the sphere cut along the surface strip. Thus the cores of the boundary annuli splice as in [F4], and this identification matches the actual diagrammatic parent, not just an unmarked abstract manifold.

Apply [F3] at all leaves and [F4] at their parent nodes, using step 2.1. Continuing upward through the finite tree proves the stronger disk property at its root. Formally, induction on the number of vertices of a finite subtree suffices: the single-vertex case is [F3], and at a nonleaf root the two smaller subtrees give the hypotheses for [F4]. This proves the property for either checkerboard when crossings are present. Together with step 1.1 it covers every diagram in the statement. All choices of annular cores give the same result: isotope the cores within their annuli and extend over a boundary collar to transport both the proper disks and their boundary disks.

To deduce geometric incompressibility, lift a hypothetical compressing disk to $N$. Its boundary is one lift of a simple closed curve $\gamma$ in $F$ and misses $s$. By steps 1.1 and 3.1 it bounds a disk on $\partial N\setminus s$. Push this disk out of the half-annular collars into the normal double cover of $F$, keeping its boundary fixed. It projects to an embedded disk in $F$: the disk and its deck translate have disjoint boundaries, and therefore are disjoint or nested unless their union is a sphere component. Each component of the normal double cover has nonempty boundary, excluding the sphere alternative. Strict nesting is incompatible with the deck involution, which would reverse that strict inclusion. Hence the disks are disjoint, so the projection is injective and bounds $\gamma$. The original disk was therefore not a compression.

By [F5], an exterior boundary compression would now yield a one-suture disk in $N$, excluded by steps 1.1 and 3.1. Thus both checkerboards are geometrically incompressible and boundary-incompressible, including for diagrams which split nontrivially in [F2].
